The Pistons defeated the Timberwolves 128-106. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Timberwolves are playing some of the best basketball in the league right now. They’ve dismantled their first three opponents by an average margin of victory of over 23 points. However, they may not have one of their star players in Monday’s game against the Cleveland Cavaliers . Minnesota added Anthony Edwards to the injury report on Monday afternoon with the designation of right knee injury management. Edwards may have tweaked that knee at the end of the second quarter of Sunday’s game against the Toronto Raptors . You can see him grimace slightly in the clip below after finishing the fast-break dunk. I’m worried about Anthony Edwards health this season 😬 pic.twitter.com/FIU0b1vwWO — Kyle Ingram (@SnapshotKyle) October 26, 2026 Support us and rep the Browns with Homage! Anything bought from the links helps support Fear the Sword . You can buy the Browns throwback shirt HERE . You can also shop all of Homage’s Cleveland gear HERE . Edwards played just 28 minutes in the Timberwolves’ 117-94 win over the Raptors on Sunday evening. He finished the night scoring 26 points on 10-of-18 shooting. Through three games, Edwards is averaging 28.7 points, 5 rebounds, and 3.3 assists per game on 44.3% shooting. Minnesota will still be a tough test for Cleveland even if Edwards can’t go. The addition of LaMelo Ball has helped elevate their offense. This is part of the reason why the Timberwolves have posted a 122.1 offensive rating ( 4th in the league ) through three games. And they still have a world-class defense with a front line that includes Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert. The rest of Minnesota’s regular starters will be available for Monday. They will, however, still be without Donte DiVincenzo, who is recovering from a right Achilles tendon injury. The Cavs will be mostly healthy for this game. Nae’Qwan Tomlin remains out with a back injury. The Cavs are still waiting for Khalifa Diop to make his debut. He’s been dealing with a left knee injury.

stories.title: Cooper Flagg upgraded to probable for Mavericks' game vs. Heat after sitting out Saturday with sprained left shoulder
stories.summary: The NBA Rookie of the Year was listed as questionable on the injury report until participating in the Mavericks' shootaround earlier on Monday.
stories.detailText: Dallas Mavericks forward Cooper Flagg has been upgraded to probable on the NBA injury report for Monday's matchup with the Miami Heat. Flagg was listed as questionable prior to the injury report released at 1 p.m. ET with a left shoulder sprain. His status was then changed to probable, likely after the second-year star participated in the Mavericks' shootaround. Cooper Flagg upgraded to probable after shootaround. pic.twitter.com/Bb7jb2TZSt — Eddie Sefko (@ESefko) October 26, 2026 The second-year star sustained a sprained left shoulder during Friday's 121-105 win over the Indiana Pacers after taking a hard foul from Aaron Nesmith as he drove to the basket. Flagg landed awkwardly on his left arm and Nesmith was called for a flagrant foul. Flagg stayed in the game to hit two free throws after the foul, but subsequently went to the locker room and did not return for the remainder of the game with what the team termed a mild shoulder sprain. He finished with 14 points, 5 rebounds, 6 assists, 3 steals and 1 block in 17 minutes. With the Mavericks scheduled for back-to-back games, Flagg sat out Saturday's 122-106 loss to the San Antonio Spurs . Originally, the team said he would be re-evaluated this week. Technically, that was correct as Flagg is apparently deemed ready to play on Monday. In his two games played, Flagg is averaging 23 points, 5 rebounds and 4 assists per game while making three of his six 3-point attempts. He scored 32 points in the Mavericks' 128-110 defeat to the Houston Rockets, becoming the youngest player in NBA history (19 years old) to score 30 or more points in a season opener . While Dallas will try to improve its record to 2-2 with a win, Miami will attempt to avoid beginning its season 0-4 for the first time since the 2007-08 season. That team lost its first five games on its way to losing eight of its first 10 games. The Heat finished 15-67 that season.

stories.title: Dream, Valkyries to play Game 6, WNBA Finals at State Farm as Thursday matinee
stories.summary: Game 6 of the WNBA Finals will be played Thursday at 12:30 p.m. ET at State Farm Arena in Atlanta. The start time of Cavs-Hawks will be pushed back to 8 p.m. ET.
stories.detailText: After a weekend of nonstop frantic discussions and negotiation, Game 6 of the WNBA Finals will be played Thursday at 12:30 p.m. ET at 17,000-seat State Farm Arena in Atlanta. The Atlanta Hawks - Cleveland Cavaliers game that night will move to 8:00 p.m. ET to accommodate the doubleheader, just as the Hawks did for Game 4. This allows a potential Game 7 to remain scheduled for Halloween at Chase Center in San Francisco. All three Finals games in Atlanta have required hurried adjustments to the schedule at State Farm Arena. It took collective efforts from the WNBA, NBA, the Hawks, State Farm Arena, Dream , Valkyries and broadcast partners to figure out the best course of action again. By moving the game earlier in the day, the WNBA avoided a scenario where a potential championship game was played inside the Dream's home arena, the 3,500-seat Gateway Center. The other option under strong consideration was moving Game 6 to an open date at State Farm Arena on Friday and Game 7 to an open date at Chase Center on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

stories.title: MMBets: Dallas will need discipline to beat the Miami Heat
stories.summary: Dusty May will have an opportunity to coach up a win on the road when the Mavericks meet the Heat at Kaseya Center.
stories.detailText: The Dallas Mavericks are in Miami playing their old rivals, the Heat, as they look for their second win of the year. Miami made a huge splash over the offseason trading for Giannis Antetokounmpo, but have not seen the fruits of their labor thus far. They have yet to win, but despite their hunger, the Mavericks are not going to go down easily. With Cooper Flagg looking good to go, Dallas can catch Miami with their pants down if they make shots early. Given the Mavericks’ center rotation, this will be Dusty May’s first true test of how he can scheme a win. It should be a chess match against one of the NBA’s longest-tenured coaches, Erik Spoelstra. Game intangibles Dallas Mavericks (1-2) at Miami Heat (0-3) Tipoff: 6:40p CT at the Kaseya Center, Miami, FL. How to watch: The game will be televised locally on KFAA Channel 29, or streaming on MavsTV+ for anyone in the Mavericks media market. For those outside of the viewing area, the game will be on NBA League Pass and NBATV. Odds via the Fanduel Sportsbook as of 2:00PM CST Spread: Dallas +7.5 (+100) Over/Under: 241.5 (-108/-112) Moneyline: Dallas +225 Player props Giannis Antetokounmpo to score 35+ points (+172) Cooper Flagg to record 8+ rebounds (+215) I think May opts for the “Luka” game plan with Giannis: let him get what he wants and take away the other guys. Miami has very little shooting around him, and letting Antetokounmpo get his 40 in the paint while everyone else is locked up will be key to keeping this close. Flagg has 10 rebounds in his last four quarters, as he had five in the second half against Houston and five in the first half against Indiana. If he can put a full game together, this should be an easy over. Game sides Dallas +7.5 (+100) Under 241.5 points (-112) Dallas has slowed the pace down in their three games. I thought the contest vs Indiana would be run-and-gun, but they kept it to a battle of execution. I think the same goes tonight in Miami. You do not want to let them get out and run; they have the better transition players. I think this will be a close, well-played game, with the Heat victorious 113-109.

stories.title: Magic's Jalen Suggs out at least 2 weeks with knee injury
stories.summary: Magic guard Jalen Suggs suffered a mild bone bruise in his right knee and will miss at least the next two weeks.
stories.detailText: Orlando Magic guard Jalen Suggs will miss at least the next two weeks after suffering a mild bone bruise in his right knee, the team announced Monday. Suggs will be reevaluated in two weeks but has avoided any major structural damage. The noncontact injury occurred late in the fourth quarter of Sunday's win over the New York Knicks . Suggs was on a breakaway fast break when his right knee appeared to buckle on his layup attempt with 2:09 remaining. Suggs stayed on the floor for several moments in pain before being helped to his feet. He walked gingerly to the Magic's locker room with help from team personnel. Suggs, the fifth pick in the 2021 draft, has averaged 12.6 points, 3.8 assists and 3.4 rebounds over his six-year career. He battled injuries the past two years that limited him to 92 games. Information from ESPN's Vincent Goodwill was used in this report.

stories.title: Knicks' honeymoon phase over already? Behind the champs' slow start
stories.summary: The Knicks are just the third defending champion in NBA history to begin the ensuing season with three consecutive losses. It didn't end well for the previous two teams.
stories.detailText: You might say that Mike Brown saw this coming. After a summer spent enjoying the spoils of helming the first New York Knicks team to win an NBA championship since the Nixon administration, the first time Brown sat down at a podium to discuss what might lay ahead in the 2026-27 campaign, the Knicks head coach repeatedly emphasized the need for his team to adhere to its established competitive standard. For his players to avoid any slippage in their day-to-day habits. For every member of the roster and staff to remain laser-focused on, and energetic in pursuit of, the process of putting themselves in position to compete for another championship. Because, the coach predicted, the hardest work was just starting. "You know, a lot of people tend to shy away from adversity — especially early on, because, you know, you get scrutinized, and sometimes it can be tough dealing with that," Brown said at the Knicks' media day session in September . "I actually yearn for it. I yearn for it early. Because I want to make sure that not only myself, but we as a group can handle it." Well, Coach, I've got good news and bad news, and they're both the same thing. That early adversity you ordered? It has officially arrived. 'It's the focus on the details' After losing to the Philadelphia 76ers on opening night , falling to the Boston Celtics on Friday and dropping a 111-102 home game to an Orlando Magic team missing injured All-Star forward Paolo Banchero on Sunday — a game they led by 10 with 9:20 remaining in the fourth quarter, before conceding a 30-9 run over the next eight-plus minutes — the Knicks sit at 0-3 on the young season, one of only seven winless teams in the Association. New York suffered just four losing streaks of three or more games all of last season . Less than a week into its title defense, that counter already sits at one. The Knicks are just the third defending champion in NBA history to begin the ensuing season with three consecutive losses, joining the 1969-70 Celtics and 2011-12 Dallas Mavericks. Those Mavericks won their fourth game , eventually finished as the West's No. 7 seed, and bowed out in the first round to the Oklahoma City Thunder. The Celtics, however, lost their fourth game , spent the entire season under .500 , and missed the playoffs for the first time in 20 years . What's past isn't necessarily prologue; the Knicks aren't destined to follow in either the Mavs' or C's footsteps. Still, though: Kind of puts a little extra mustard on the outcome of New York's Tuesday night tilt with the Detroit Pistons, doesn't it? Those Pistons — who finished with the No. 1 seed in the East last season, and who swept the Knicks by an average of 28 points per game during the regular season — improved to 3-0 on Sunday with a 106-93 road win over the Sixers. They figure to be champing at the bit for a shot at the champs … and, even without injured All-NBA center Jalen Duren , eminently capable of knocking the Knicks' lights out if New York can't find the 48 minutes' worth of tighten-the-screws attention to detail, crispness and physicality that Brown acknowledges has thus far eluded his club. "It's the focus on the details," Brown told reporters after Sunday's loss. "You know, you go on a run, and then you come down and you throw the ball away. Like, probably three-fourths of our turnovers weren't from [the Magic's] pressure — and again, that's nothing against them, they beat us, I give them a lot of credit — but we throw the ball [low], we throw the ball and it goes through our hands, we jump in the air … and those turnovers, they convert the other way." After averaging 13.6 turnovers per game during the 2025-26 regular season, and 13.5 cough-ups a contest in the playoffs , New York has given it up 16.3 times a night thus far . That increase in turnovers is the primary reason why the Knicks' margin in the possession battle has dropped from +2.9 possessions per game last season, according to Jared Dubin's analysis at Last Night in Basketball , to +1.9 through three games — still good, but not elite. Combine that with Knicks opponents averaging 20.7 points per game off those turnovers — more than four points per game more than last season — and the margins that New York often mastered last season en route to 53 wins, a top-six point differential and eventually a title have grown considerably thinner. "We do a pretty good job on some of the closeouts, and then other closeouts, we stop short, especially to a hot guy, and we let him shoot a comfortable shot," Brown said. "We play great defense, make them take a tough shot, and then we don't box out. Those are the little things that we've got to continue to embrace — especially when we're not shooting the ball well." New York's shooting woes The Knicks are most certainly not shooting the ball well right now. Their offensive process, by and large, hasn't been bad. The Knicks are generating a higher share of their shots at the rim this year than last while also taking an above-league-average percentage of their attempts from 3-point range — including the NBA's highest rate of corner 3s, which have accounted for 14% of New York's total field-goal attempts through three games, according to Cleaning the Glass . Which is to say: The Knicks have broadly been creating a lot of the right kinds of looks, ranking in the top 10 in multiple shot quality and expected field-goal percentage metrics. The issue is, they're just not making many of them. Through three games, the Knicks are shooting about 3% worse at the rim, 5% worse from 3-point land, and 16% worse on midrange tries than they did last season . Only one Knick, Karl-Anthony Towns, has made more than half of his shots; the other four members of New York's vaunted starting five have all been slow to get their shots online coming out of the gate. Jalen Brunson is putting the Knicks' early-season struggles on his shoulders. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) Maddie Meyer via Getty Images Jalen Brunson, who spent much of his summer rehabilitating after undergoing surgery on his shooting wrist , sits under 40% from the field. OG Anunoby and Josh Hart are just barely above that mark. Mikal Bridges, whose mid-postseason turnaround was so vital to the Knicks' torrid run through the East during the springtime, has been positively frigid out of the gates: 5-for-23 from the field and 0-for-10 from 3-point range, for just 10 points in 90 minutes across three games. All told, only the Chicago Bulls, Miami Heat and Toronto Raptors are underperforming their expected shot quality by more than the Knicks thus far, according to Synergy Sports Technology. That frozen start goes a long way toward explaining how a Knicks team that has ranked in the top seven in offensive efficiency in each of the last four seasons currently sits a dismal 29th in points scored per possession, and dead stinkin' last in half-court scoring efficiency . Brunson spoke Sunday about the Knicks' need to tighten up their organization in the half-court — getting to the right spots, at the right pace, to execute properly and create the openings that can lead to cleaner looks and better scoring chances — which, ultimately, rests with their superstar point guard. "Everything falls on my shoulders," said Brunson, who scored a team-high 28 points on 28 shot attempts against Orlando, in the Knicks' locker room after the loss. "I've just got to be a better leader when it comes to that, when it comes to making sure our guys are ready to go and in the right spots. There's a lot of other little things, but that's the main thing. It's just organization on my part." That lack of organization and precision has been particularly notable in close-and-late situations, in which the Knicks — and Brunson, in particular — performed so brilliantly last season. New York has been outscored by a league-high 18 points in 10 minutes of "clutch" time thus far this season, according to NBA Advanced Stats , scoring well under one point per possession with more turnovers (four) than assists (two). Brunson has missed five of his seven shots in those high-leverage moments — emblematic of the run of play for a Knicks squad that has thus far only intermittently resembled the team that locked into such an incredible offensive rhythm last postseason. "We're not going to be the same," Brunson said. "We're not going to be the way we were playing last year. That's just human nature. But we have to accept this part of the journey, find a way to be better, and hopefully throughout a couple of games, we'll be able to look back and say, 'Hey, we grew from that.'" Will the Knicks turn it around? The schedule does afford some get-right opportunities. After Tuesday's matchup with the undefeated Pistons, New York will play four of its next six games against the Chicago Bulls, Brooklyn Nets and Milwaukee Bucks — teams with a combined 1-8 record. Thaw out those jumpers a bit and get some regression to the mean in the overall shot-making, and New York could relocate its rhythm in a flash. On the other hand, though, the Knicks feel a long way from prematurely marking those down as wins given the way they're misfiring right now. "Games like [Sunday's loss to the Magic] will tell us that, you know, like I said before, our crap stinks," Brown said. "It does. And we're the only ones that can do something about it. There's no light switch that we can just turn on and think that we're going to go win ballgames. Nobody's going to give us anything." No, the Knicks will have to take the wins they need to right the ship — and, as Brunson stressed, they'll have to do it by sticking together. "One thing I said throughout the entire training camp, and honestly to this day, is: we're going to see who we are within the first couple of weeks of the season," Brunson said Sunday. "We're hitting adversity now. How are we going to respond?" They need a collective response. Better shooting across the board. Better physicality at the point of attack from Bridges and Anunoby. Better foul avoidance from Towns, who's averaging a career-high 4.6 personals per 36 minutes. Better play in the middle when Towns hits the bench, with Andre Drummond coming back down to Earth after his strong first half in the season opener against Philly and James Wiseman providing up-and-down minutes on Sunday against Orlando. Better everything, really. Except, maybe, better treatment from the adoring masses who spent the summer throwing flowers at the Knicks' feet. "Everyone's been telling us what a great job we did — how fun it was, what we did for the city, the constant praise," Brunson said. "We need kind of, just … the opposite." Well, Cap, I've got good news and bad news, and they're both the same thing. Keep playing like this, and the honeymoon period of that constant praise might be over a hell of a lot sooner than anybody anticipated.

stories.title: The Biggest Change for the Wolves This Season
stories.summary: The Minnesota Timberwolves are already seeing a drastic difference in their approach through two games this season.
stories.detailText: ORLANDO, FL - OCTOBER 23: Jonathan Kuminga #24 of the Minnesota Timberwolves grabs the rebound during the game against the Orlando Magic on October 23, 2026 at Kia Center in Orlando, Florida. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Fernando Medina/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images It’s a small sample size, but the Minnesota Timberwolves lead the league in rebounding after the first three games this season. The Wolves hauled in 52 boards against the Miami Heat, 61 against the Orlando Magic, and 49 against the Toronto Raptors . In all three contests, the Wolves dominated the glass, and it led to three blowout victories. Wolves head coach Chris Finch explained why there has been a shift in the team’s approach to rebounding over the weekend. “It starts with Jaden (McDaniels) and Anthony (Edwards) and JK (Jonathan Kuminga). Those guys just getting back in the play and rebounding the ball in the air. We’ve been harping on it,” Finch said. “Obviously, it’s easier to rebound when you play really good kind of first-shot defense, and you can force them into shots where you’re not in rotations and stuff like that, so that’s been key to it as well – being able to be in good help spots and then go pursue the ball. That’s really what it is. It’s the pursuit of the ball on both ends of the floor. We were one of the worst teams in terms of watching rebounds and not actually pursuing the ball, and this year we’ve been able to switch our mentality to be more of a pursuit team.” Crashing the glass on the offensive side of the ball has increased the number of possessions Minnesota gets. The more shots they’re taking, the more are falling. If the Wolves can continue this mindset across the course of the season, they should be one of the biggest threats in the Western Conference. Many thought that the loss of Naz Reid and Julius Randle would hurt the team’s rebounding efforts, but going smaller in the lineup has forced everybody to prioritize rebounding when they are on the court. The Timberwolves lead the NBA in net rebounding. So much for the losing Julius Randle size bit pic.twitter.com/J1WWZxLHMn — Bull Run (@run_bull_) October 24, 2026 Wolves center Rudy Gobert emphasized the importance of all five players contributing to the rebounding efforts and how much of a difference it is making. “I think just compete, and just having the mindset of doing something… whatever is happening on the floor, finding a body, contesting the shots and I think it goes from one to five,” Gobert said. “Having five guys doing something… being active, and when we do that, it makes it easy for me, and it makes it easy for us as a team.” It’s going to be difficult to keep up this trend, but this could be what sets the Wolves apart from their competitors.

stories.title: Magic's Jalen Suggs diagnosed with bone bruise in right knee, will be re-evaluated in 2 weeks
stories.summary: Jalen Suggs' knee buckled as he was going up for a layup on Sunday night at Madison Square Garden.
stories.detailText: Jalen Suggs has avoided a major injury after all. The Orlando Magic guard went down with a non-contact knee injury in their win over the New York Knicks on Sunday night. But an MRI on Monday revealed Suggs only suffered a "mild bone bruise" in his right knee, the team announced . As a result, he will be re-evaluated in two weeks. While that's still a significant stretch, it's far better than the season-ending injury many had feared after seeing him go down. Suggs avoided any major structural damage to the knee, per the team. INJURY UPDATE: @OrlandoMagic guard Jalen Suggs underwent an MRI, which revealed a mild right knee bone bruise. There was no other structural damage. He will be reevaluated in two weeks. Suggs suffered the injury during the fourth quarter of last night’s game at New York. — Orlando Magic PR (@Magic_PR) October 26, 2026 Suggs went up for what should have been an easy fast-break layup at Madison Square Garden in the fourth quarter of their 111-102 win on Sunday night. But as he went up, his right knee buckled. Suggs fell to the ground after missing the shot. He immediately reached for his knee and started rolling around in pain underneath the basket. He remained down for quite some time, but was eventually helped up and limped off the court while barely putting any weight on his leg. NOT what the Magic needed. Jalen Suggs goes down clutching his right knee going up for a layup without contact. @DanteMagic and Jeff Turner were right on it to not speculate the injury. But not good for the Magic who have terrible injury luck pic.twitter.com/dGyAB6D7Cd — Zach Maskavich WESH (@ZachMaskavich) October 26, 2026 The Magic didn't have an update on Suggs' condition after the game. Coach Sean Sweeney was hopeful he just hyperextended his knee and said Suggs was in good spirits after the contest. Suggs finished with four points, six rebounds and six assists in the win. The former No. 5 overall pick is in his sixth season. He averaged 13.8 points and 5.5 assists per game last season while helping the Magic reach the playoffs for a third straight year. Despite losing Suggs and star Paolo Banchero already out with an ankle sprain, the Magic held on to beat the Knicks on Sunday night to secure their first win of the season. They are now 1-2 entering Wednesday's contest against the Toronto Raptors in Canada. But losing Suggs will undoubtedly make things much more difficult for the Magic as the season gets going.

stories.title: JJ Redick had fun watching ‘showman’ Luka Dončić against Jazz
stories.summary: The Slovenian put on a sensational performance Sunday
stories.detailText: SALT LAKE CITY, UTAH - OCTOBER 25 : Luka Doncic #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers hushes the crowd after sinking a three pointer against the Utah Jazz during the second half of their game at the Delta Center on October 25, 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Chris Gardner/ Getty Images) | Getty Images In fitting fashion, last year’s scoring champ, Luka Dončić, dropped the first 50-piece of the 2026-27 season with a 52-point, 10-assist, eight-rebound performance Sunday against the Utah Jazz. It was his fourth career game with at least 50 points, 10 assists and five rebounds to give him sole possession of the second-most such games in NBA history. He was particularly sensational in crunch time as t he Los Angeles Lakers looked to secure an 18-point comeback and win their third straight contest to open the year. Over the final seven minutes of the game, Dončić tallied 13 points and two assists. He directly contributed to 19 of the Lakers’ last 24 points with plays like these: LUKA'S GOT 42 PTS 🔥 He sinks his 6th TRIPLE! The Lakers and Jazz are TIED in Q4 on NBA League Pass 🍿 pic.twitter.com/yAsT6gxWXl — NBA (@NBA) October 25, 2026 “I think, for him in particular, when he’s in the flow state, he gets into like showman mode,” head coach JJ Redick said. “He’s on stage performing and it’s always really fun to watch,” Aside from a Collin Sexton triple midway through the fourth quarter, the only other non-Dončić player to score across the final seven minutes was Austin Reaves, whose six crunch-time points, including a late clock three to seal the win, helped keep Utah at bay. Reaves himself was pretty excellent Sunday to maintain his sterling play out of the gates this season. He scored 29 points on 81.8% true shooting while chipping in four assists, two blocks and one steal. Despite his own superlatives, however, he sounds completely content to let Dončić cook when the Slovenian is in the sort of groove he found against the Jazz. “Once he gets in the mode he gets in, it’s just give him the ball and he’s either going to put the ball in basket or he’s going to make the right [play],” Reaves said. “I just happened to be open and he threw it to me, was open, shot it with confidence and made it. “He’s always in showman mode. I think he’s always ready to get a bucket. Knowing that as a teammate, you just let him do him and we’re going to benefit from it as a team.” You can follow Jackson on Twitter at @jackfrank_jjf .

stories.title: Roundtable: Early Overreactions to Mavericks Basketball
stories.summary: Feelings over facts, if you please
stories.detailText: HOUSTON, TX - OCTOBER 21: Sergio de Larrea #55 of the Dallas Mavericks looks on during the game against the Houston Rockets on October 21, 2026 at the Toyota Center in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Garrett Ellwood/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images With a game Saturday night, then all Sunday and all of today between the game tonight, we didn’t have a ton in the hopper to publish. So I gave a simple prompt: please overreact to the first three games of Dallas Mavericks basketball. Sudarshan : Cooper Flagg will make 1 of the All-NBA teams (I predict All-NBA 3rd team), and depending on how much game time he gets, Sergio De Larrea will make the All-Rookie 1st team. Flagg has come out of the blocks all guns blazing to start the season, and Larry was so good against San Antonio that Mavs internet is already squinting and trying to make Luka Doncic comparisons. ¡Viva la youth revolución! Also, Aaron Nesmith needs to hire a bodyguard to protect himself from Bryan when he comes to play in Dallas. Bryan : The individual player skill development most important to long-term winning for the Mavs is no longer Cooper’s shooting: it’s now Sergio’s ball handling. If Larry becomes a good enough ball handler to take on a primary role even off the bench by midway through next year, that will more than mitigate not having our own 2027 first-round pick because he’s already an NBA player in every other skill that matters. If he continues to progress as he’s shown from summer league to now, we are going to look at the 2027 draft class and be able to count on one hand the number of players that we’re sure are better than him. Gracie : I will go further than Sudarshan, Cooper Flagg will be in MVP talks. He took over for the Mavericks in their loss to Houston, showing that he has taken another step offensively after a strong rookie year. Before he was hurt against Indiana, he was on pace for a 30-point triple-double. His two-way skills set the tone for Dallas. He has emerged as a leader for the Mavericks, and the team is significantly better when he’s on the floor. His willingness to grow as a player and a leader will have him getting nods for MVP of the Mavericks can make the postseason. Eric : Sergio deLarrea might be the draft-night steal of 2026. Twenty-one points, five rebounds, and four assists against San Antonio. He looked comfortable running the offense against one of the league’s toughest young defensive backcourts. Joe : I don’t know how this isn’t EVERYONE’S overreaction, but PJ looks back to PJ. Now that doesn’t mean he looks like this all-world role player who is gonna be the difference in us winning X amount of games compared to Y amount of games, but also the team isn’t really good enough for him to be that piece anyway. But PJ has looked really surprisingly competent and has been really impactful through 3 games. He’s been hitting shots, getting to the rim at will, playing solid defense and rebounding, and has been the best player for the Mavs when Kyrie and/or Cooper aren’t out there. He’s averaging 14 points and has knocked down 40% combined from 3 in the second and third games. Tyler : Let’s dive into some small sample size theater, shall we? The PJ Washington, Naji Marshall and Max Christie minutes need to GO. Per Cleaning the Glass, in 87 possessions together, those lineups are -42.5 points per 100 possessions, with an offensive rating of 82.8. The vets have been good soldiers over the last couple of turbulent seasons, but we can officially close the book on them now. Conversely, the two-man unit of Cooper Flagg and Zaccharie Risacher are +81.5 points per 100 possessions in 54 total possessions. The youth movement is here, so let’s lean in to it! Michael : My overreaction to the first three games is that Masai Ujiri and Mike Schmitz are much better at maximizing limited assets than anyone gave them credit for. Sergio de Larrea looked like a seasoned player against one of the best teams in the West. His first two games weren’t the prettiest, but I chalk that up to getting acclimated. Meaning, I think what we saw from him against San Antonio is more the true version of him than not. Marcus Sasser is another one. A forgotten man in Detroit, he comes home to Dallas and fits in immediately, playing within himself and able to score off the bench and hit the long ball with consistency. All to say my overreaction is that the front office is equipped to make good things happen even with limited resources. Kirk : This isn’t an overreaction in so much as something I need more of: the three guard line up. Play a mix of Kyrie, Sergio, Sasser, and Walter, please. Matt M. : Well, you asked for overreaction, so here we go. The Mavs have turned over a few rocks, and the guard play they have found stuck to the bottom of those rocks has been intriguing enough so that I am now more curious what Dallas can get in a trade for Kyrie Irving than I am about what wisdom he can impart to a squad of youngsters. I like what I’ve seen from Marcus Sasser, Sergio de Larrea, and even Walter Clayton Jr. (yes, I know he’s not full-time but there are solutions for everything) to such a degree that I am beginning to wonder if the best use of Irving this year is not a salute and an expression of heartfelt gratitude while ushering him out the door in exchange for a tasty first-round pick and a usable younger guard. Full-on youth movement now, please. Trink : My overreaction is this team is one point guard away from being a legit playoff team. If they can have someone relieve Kyrie of ball handling in the starting five, they have a legit chance to be a 6 seed or higher. Cooper Flagg refuses to lose, and the team will come with him.

stories.title: How Jalen Williams’ gruesome leg injury could alter Thunder’s title hopes
stories.summary: Oklahoma City Thunder star Jalen Williams suffered a serious lower leg injury. So how does this change the path forward for the title favorites?
stories.detailText: It became clear it was so bad – even in the first seconds after it happened – that a trainer rushed over to throw a towel over the ankle, hiding it from view. Oklahoma City Thunder star Jalen Williams, a 2024-25 All-Star and one of the bright young players in the NBA, suffered a seemingly devastating lower leg injury Sunday, Oct. 25. And though the Thunder haven’t issued a formal diagnosis, the way Williams’ left ankle dangled sideways off his foot strongly suggests that Williams’ season is over just three games after it started. So now the Thunder, who entered the season as favorites to win NBA Finals, must regroup, because this injury – assuming it’s as bad as it looked – changes the pathway for Oklahoma City moving forward. Because the overwhelming notion for this Thunder team was that it was a strong favorite because Williams was finally healthy. Williams, the team’s second best player, missed significant chunks last season as he recovered from offseason wrist surgery. Then, late in the year and into the playoffs, it was multiple soft-tissue hamstring injuries . So now, two-time reigning Most Valuable Player Shai Gilgeous-Alexander , once again, will have bear more of a burden. Williams can handle the ball and initiate offense. He can slash to the basket and has a dependable perimeter jumper. He’s a plus defender and is often the anchor through which the Thunder run their offense when Gilgeous-Alexander is catching a breath on the bench. When available, he is a staple, having started 238 of his 251 career regular season games. The loss is massive. "These are tough, man," Thunder coach Mark Daigneault said after the game. "We’re not doing great. That’s tough on the guys. Everyone empathizes, I think both teams, in those situations. We’re not doing great." Yet, if there is any team in the NBA built to weather the loss of a player like Williams, it’s the Thunder. No team has been better at identifying and developing young players through the draft, and Oklahoma City is the deepest team in the entire association. They have options. Thunder's depth provides options after Jalen Williams injury In fact, the Thunder are so deep that they can alter whom they start at small forward in place of Williams, depending on the matchup. The first indication of how the Thunder plan to make up for the loss of Williams comes fewer than 24 hours after he suffered the injury; Oklahoma City hosts the Phoenix Suns Monday, Oct. 26 on the second leg of their back-to-back. The cleanest move is for Daigneault to replace Williams in the starting lineup with Alex Caruso , a veteran guard who specializes on defense. Caruso is nowhere near as talented as Williams on offense, though his perimeter shot has been a spark off the bench; Caruso is shooting a blistering 45.5% from 3-point range this season. Each of starting guard Cason Wallace , who also suffered an injury Sunday night, one to his shoulder, and reserve guards Ajay Mitchell and Jared McCain will likely see increased minutes and responsibility. Daigneault likes to have a serviceable ball-handling creator on the floor when Gilgeous-Alexander heads to the bench, so it makes sense on some level for both Mitchell and McCain to come off the bench. Rookie guard Bennett Stirtz will also be called up for spot minutes. Thunder's injury history prepared SGA, team to weather long season This, unfortunately for the Thunder, is a familiar spot. They pushed the San Antonio Spurs to seven games in the 2026 Western Conference Finals despite injuries to Williams and Mitchell. Because the pair are Oklahoma City’s best offensive engines not named Gilgeous-Alexander, the team’s offense stagnated under San Antonio’s defense. In previous seasons, it was Chet Holmgren and Isaiah Hartenstein who were knocked out for extensive stretches because of injury. This is all to say that, in many ways, the Thunder are used to this. But as much as Oklahoma City is built to mitigate the loss of a star like Williams, one devastating fact is clear, and it’s a fact the team must contend with the rest of the season, assuming the injury ends Williams’ campaign. The Thunder today are not as strong as they were yesterday, and that’s indisputable. stories.title: The Knicks are too talented to keep playing like this offensively
stories.summary: Reason A, B, and C as to why the Knicks are 0-3 has to do with their expensive roster not making shots.
stories.detailText: BOSTON, MASSACHUSETTS - OCTOBER 23: Jalen Brunson #11 of the New York Knicks looks on during second half of the Celtics Home Opener at TD Garden on October 23, 2026 in Boston, Massachusetts. The Celtics defeat the Knicks 107-103. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) | Getty Images When people said they wouldn’t care if the Knicks went 0-82 this season, I don’t think that they meant it as an invitation. The first three games have gone from disappointing to annoying to bewildering as the Knicks sit at the bottom of the standings with a 0-3 record after three close losses to Eastern Conference rivals, all of which were winnable with better execution. It’s the first 0-3 start since David Fizdale was coach in 2019-20 (yikes). In these games, the Knicks have scored 103 or fewer points in all of them. Raw point totals aren’t everything with this team’s preferred slow pace, but that doesn’t work in the modern NBA. This is early-Thibsian-level offense. Is it process-based or just shoddy shooting? It could be both. On Opening Night, the Knicks fell to the Sixers not only due to inconsistent shooting at the perimeter, but also startlingly bad finishing at the rim. As a team last year, they shot 66.3% in the restricted area and 58.3% on shots in the paint. On Opening Night? 58.6% and 42%. These shots make up half the team’s shot diet, so shooting 16% worse at it can decide games. That’s especially concerning against a team with incredibly little rim protection, even if it were the freshest Joel Embiid you’ll ever see. The jarringly bad shooting continued through Boston and Orlando. They’re 26th in FG% at the restricted area (63%) and dead last in total FG% in the paint (50%). The main culprits? Andre Drummond (8-for-15 at the rim, 8-for-18 in the paint), Jalen Brunson (4-for-18 outside the restricted area), and Josh Hart (4-for-8 at the rim, 7-for-13 in the paint). Those last two are the ones we can directly compare to last season. Brunson shot 47.9% on incredible volume outside the restricted area last season, while Hart shot 67.4% at the rim and 60.4% in the entire paint. The sample is small, but important in three close losses. The perimeter shooting has been pretty bad, too. Outside of Deuce McBride’s Boston heater, nobody has had the touch to start the season. Four players have attempted at least 14 threes so far, and all of them are below league average (Brunson 26.7%, Anunoby 28.6%, Hart 33.3%, Shamet 35.7%). Mikal Bridges is also doing his best October 2024 impression, starting the year 0-for-10 from deep. On Sunday night against the Magic, the Knicks shot 32 open and wide open threes and made only nine of them. There were some bad looks in there, but a lot of them were clean looks that you’re used to them making. Last season, they only averaged 30.5 of those attempts per game, but shot 37.3%. That’s equivalent to three extra made threes last night, which could’ve swung the game. Really, they lost on Sunday because the Magic, an extremely poor shooting team, shot 43.6% on those looks and had just their third game in the last two years where they shot 40 threes and made at least 40% of them, but you could’ve also made shots yourself. As if their shooting at the rim and behind the arc wasn’t bad enough, they’ve also been ghastly at the foul line. As a team, they’re shooting 70.8%, which in prior years you’d think would be dragged down by the Hack-a-Mitch, but there’s no excuse this year. Even if you remove the only poor free-throw shooter on the roster, Drummond, they’re at an unacceptable 72%. If you removed Mitch last year, the team shot 81.6% from the line. It added up against Philly; it didn’t help against Boston; and it directly hampered their chances at a late comeback against Orlando. Anunoby is at 81.8%, but after him? Brunson is 14-for-20, and Towns is 12-for-17, both around 70%. For two guys who are career 85% free-throw shooters, it’s a back-breaker. Looking at the splits (and turnovers, which are also a small problem) through three games, the Knicks aren’t close to where they need to be as a team: vs PHI: 37/33/70, 14 TO @ BOS: 44/40/71, 16 TO vs ORL: 41/24/68, 14 TO – 25-26: 48/37/79, 12.9 TO The only game they shot adequately was against Boston, but they committed a season high in turnovers and still didn’t make their free throws. In the other two games, it was poor play at all three levels. In the modern NBA, three-point shooting is everything. For the Knicks under Mike Brown, they are as reliant as a team can be without being Joe Mazzulla-esque. 2025-26 Knicks, including playoffs: 22-0 when shooting 44% or better 0-7 when shooting 25% or worse Last season, when the Knicks shot worse than 33.3% from downtown, they went 11-19. When they shot 33.3% or better, a mark that is not even league average, they went 58-13. It’s a cheat code for their success, and considering they returned every shooter from last season’s roster, it’s one that needs to show up to right the ship.

stories.title: Game Preview #4: Wolves at Cavaliers Game Thread
stories.summary: Minnesota looks to continue on their quest for 82-0 on a back-to-back in Cleveland.
stories.detailText: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - JANUARY 18: Anthony Edwards #5 of the Minnesota Timberwolves embraces Donovan Mitchell #45 of the Cleveland Cavaliers after the game against the Cleveland Cavaliers on January 18, 2025 at Target Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Coach Chris Finch rewarded the effort of his squad with frequent breathers and deployed 11 players in non-garbage minutes. Some of this was due to LaMelo Ball foul trouble. Or was that Melo’s strategy all along for saving his legs for the next day? Minnesota’s opponent the Cleveland Cavaliers are struggling to find their Eastern Conference Finalist form in the early goings of the season. They will have the advantages of rest and home court as they host the undefeated Wolves. Game Info Who: Minnesota Timberwolves (3-0) vs. Cleveland Cavaliers (1-1) When: Monday, October 26 at 6:00 PM CT Where: Rocket Arena – Cleveland, OH Local TV: DAZN-MIN Radio: 830 WCCO Some Numbers Playing for Each Other MINNEAPOLIS, MN – OCTOBER 25: Anthony Edwards #5 celebrates with Ayo Dosunmu #13 of the Minnesota Timberwolves during the game against the Toronto Raptors on October 25, 2026 at Target Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Jordan Johnson/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Maybe it was something in the Parisian water. Maybe it was the iron sharpening iron team organized practices before training camp. Maybe it was the trade for LaMelo Ball and the full court press to get Jonathan Kuminga to sign in Minnesota. Whatever it was, this Wolves team is knit tighter and more defined than a Norwegian sweater. No matter the lineup that Finch runs out, every player knows what is expected of them. In the Raptors game, every player bought in on relentless defense regardless of assignment as seen most prominently in Bones Hyland posting as many points as he did blocks and rebounds (three of each). The early efforts have taken some of the load off the regular rotation and allowed the deep bench to get some run. Rookie Isaiah Evans has played in each of the first three wins. These Wolves are not playing with their food. When they build a lead they add to it. They have only lost three quarters thus far and two of those were in the fourth quarter of 20+ point victories. Even the players “sitting” on the bench understand what is expected of them. Apr 20, 2026; Cleveland, Ohio, USA; Cleveland Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell (45) talks with guard James Harden (1) during the first half during game two of the first round of the 2026 NBA Playoffs against the Toronto Raptors at Rocket Arena. Mandatory Credit: David Dermer-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Target the Bad Defenders The Cavaliers deploy two bigs in Jarrett Allen and Evan Mobley who will roam the paint looking to swat shots. Cleveland has averaged eight and a half blocks in their two games, good enough for first in the league. They outbid the Denver Nuggets in a sign-and-trade for Peyton Watson to defend on the wing, and that’s where the strength of their defense trails off. James Harden presents some effort when he can guard in the post, but when asked to move his feet, he runs into problems. As the Wolves did against the Miami Heat’s Klay Thompson, they should hunt the Harden and Donovan Mitchell on the perimeter. The rest of the Cavs rely on the shot creation of those two players to get their offense going, so pulling them into a recurrent defensive stance will wear them out. Off the bench, Cleveland relies on the scoring of wings Jaylon Tyson, Sam Merrill, and former Trey Lyles Real Madrid teammate Mario Hezonja, none of whom offer much more defensive resistance than who they replace. Rebounds and Turnovers The Raptors won the offensive rebounding and turnover battle against the Wolves allowing them to hang around until early in the third quarter. I’d imagine Finch and the coaching staff will be in the player’s ears on the flight to Ohio about ways to clean that up. This will be a unique test for the Wolves playing on the second night of a back-to-back. They rank number one in the league in rebounding, predicated on effort and gang rebounding. They will need to summon that same sweat equity to nullify Cleveland’s bigs. The Cavaliers have choked away one game against the Philadelphia 76ers and barely hung on against the Brooklyn Nets with fourth quarter turnovers. They have coughed up the ball over 20+ times in each of their first two games with Mitchell and Harden among the biggest culprits. Perhaps a student of the Shaquille O’Neal school of taking the season to play into shape, Harden has shown limited burst to get to the cup. Staying in front of him should allow for off-ball defenders to swarm passing lanes and juice the score in transition. Prediction The Wolves have momentum, a clear thesis of what they want to do, and the spirit of youth. The Cavs guards will look to put Minnesota into compromising positions and if the Wolves play clean, they’ll run out to an early lead. Off of tired legs, less Wolves three-balls will drop, but second efforts on the glass will sap the confidence of their opponent. Cleveland will try to get back into the game launching errant three-point shots and Cavs coach Kenny Atkinson will assure the media that by every number but the final score, they won the game. Isaiah Evans will record his first regular season point. Our blogging buddies are over at Fear the Sword . Be respectful of our sword swinging brethren!

(Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Phoenix Suns’ first two games of the season couldn’t have gone more differently. A historic beatdown from the Portland Trail Blazers commenced their season, which they followed up three days later with a solid victory over a Stephen Curry-less Golden State Warriors team in their home opener. Nonetheless, it was a 1-1 week despite losing by 41 in their first game. The beauty of a singular game only being worth one loss, no matter the outcome. Now having our first glimpse of the 2026-27 regular season Suns, here’s what we want your responses on: Thoughts on the new guys Luke Kennard and Miles Bridges are in Phoenix and contributing early. While Kennard didn’t play in the season opener and Bridges scored just eight points on 3-of-11 shooting, both were impactful in the team’s first win of the season. Kennard hit three three-pointers, including a few late, and Bridges showed his inside-out game, scoring in the paint and hitting a few triples against the Warriors. How do you think the two have fit in so far, and how do you expect their roles to evolve as the season goes on? Starting guard drama looming? Early returns on the Jalen Green and Devin Booker starting backcourt have not been promising. The first game of the season saw the Suns go down 21-0 en route to getting blown out, and in 13 minutes against the Warriors, the starting lineup had a -21.6 net rating. In comparison, when Collin Gillespie was replaced by Green, the rest of the starting lineup had a +85.7 net rating. Two games into a season is no time for seismic changes, and the Suns as a whole mightily struggled in their first game of the season especially, but how concerned are you about Jalen Green’s fit next to Devin Booker in the starting lineup? Early returns on Khaman Maluach as the starter? There’s a new starting center in Phoenix, and his name is Khaman Maluach, and he’s been quite passive on the offensive end so far. In 44 minutes in his first two games, the Duke product has taken just five shots and six free throws, averaging 5.5 points, 7.5 rebounds, and two assists per game. As the team continues to play without a traditional point guard in the starting lineup, it might take Maluach some time to find his role on the offensive end, and his 136.4 defensive rating leaves a lot to be desired on defense, but the team has been significantly better on the glass when he’s in the game. It was well-known that the big man was going to take some time to get comfortable in his new role, but have early returns given you more or less confidence in his future as a starter? On the Suns’ Plate This Week Another two-game slate this week starting on the road and ending at home against the Western Conference for the Suns. Phoenix will face the Oklahoma City Thunder tonight at 5 PM AZ time in a rematch of the first round of the 2026 Western Conference Playoffs that saw the Suns go down in four games. Then on Friday, they’ll host the Denver Nuggets at 7 PM AZ time for their first game of NBA Cup play. The Thunder and Nuggets were the West’s first and third seeds a season ago and once again project to be some of the conference’s best teams.

stories.title: The Lakers got an early reference point in comeback win over the Jazz
stories.summary: Despite falling behind by 18 in the first quarter, the Lakers maintained a perfect record to open the year
stories.detailText: SALT LAKE CITY, UTAH - OCTOBER 25 : Head Coach JJ Redick talks with Luka Doncic #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers during the second half of their game against the Utah Jazz at the Delta Center on October 25, 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Chris Gardner/ Getty Images) | Getty Images By first quarter’s end on Sunday, the Los Angeles Lakers looked a bit of a mess and trailed the Utah Jazz, 47-29. By halftime, they had righted the ship and already stormed all the way back to enter the break with a 74-71 lead. For much of the second half, the two sides engaged in a back-and-forth affair before Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves made a handful of key plays down the stretch to propel Los Angeles to a 132-123 victory and a 3-o start to the year. After the win, head coach JJ Redick emphasized the importance of a game like that so early in the season for a team still growing together with so many new rotation players. Of course, doing so in a win is preferable but Redick made clear it would’ve provided valuable information regardless of the outcome. “I talked about this earlier in the year last year. For, particularly, a new group of guys and this feels like a newer team, right, because of all the new faces, you need to build reference,” Redick told reporters. “Really, whether we had responded to the adversity of that first quarter, not being ready to play and not doing any of the stuff that we had talked about pregame, it still would be a reference point. Because we ended up coming back and winning, now it becomes a positive reference point and it’s a reference point for resiliency, right?” Once Utah had built an 18-point advantage to close the first quarter, Redick saw his team quickly respond in the second quarter to extinguish the deficit and, ultimately, nab a road victory — something that shouldn’t be discounted, especially against a team that’s given the Lakers trouble in recent years. “Winning on the road is hard in the NBA. These guys always play us tough, particularly here, at least since I’ve been here,” Redick said. “So I wasn’t surprised with how they came out and played offensively. But our guys were, we talked to them at the beginning of the second quarter and there was an immediate response and then we had to gut out a win. We had to gut out a win and I’m just proud of the group for that.” You can follow Jackson on Twitter at @jackfrank_jjf .

stories.title: Maxey named East Player of the Week for standout start to season
stories.summary: Tyrese Maxey earned another award at the very start of the 2026-27 season.
stories.detailText: Maxey named East Player of the Week for standout start to season originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia True to form, All-NBA Sixers guard Tyrese Maxey earned another award at the very start of the 2026-27 season. Maxey was named the NBA’s Eastern Conference Player of the Week on Monday. The Grizzlies’ Ty Jerome won the award in the Western Conference. Maxey averaged 28.8 points, 4.8 assists and 4.0 rebounds for the new-look, 3-1 Sixers. He posted at least 26 points in all four games and ranks fifth in the NBA in scoring average. The 25-year-old also impressed on defense. He’s already racked up eight steals and his full-court pressure on former teammate James Harden helped fuel the Sixers’ home-opening comeback win last Thursday over the Cavs. “He totally changed the game,” Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. “He’s out there doing that and the rest of the guys are in the back watching. And all of a sudden, they start saying, ‘I’ll be in on this, too.’ “He provides not only the physical effort to start it, but also kind of a spark that got everyone emotionally going.” Maxey has won five East Player of the Week awards in his career. His first also came in Week 1. Maxey took home the honor in late October of 2023 right before the Sixers traded Harden to the Clippers.

stories.title: How Payton Pritchard became Boston's unlikely iso king
stories.summary: The sixth man supreme doggedly sharpens his game in brutal summer practices. That's an edge the C's will need.
stories.detailText: PAYTON PRITCHARD IS at the Celtics bench when he feels a tap on his shoulder. It's late April, and time is running out in Game 3 of the first round of the playoffs. Boston has padded its lead to 103-98 with just over a minute to go, and a win on the road in Philadelphia is in sight. That's what the Celtics usually do, after all: beat the Sixers in the playoffs, every time they've met in the postseason in the past 44 years. Pritchard has rained 3s tonight, five in all, to help with their latest effort, so who knows what kind of Philly-cooked hospitality awaits Pritchard right now. He turns to find a man even shorter than he is -- a rarity for Pritchard on NBA courts -- who is swathed in all black. Black leather jacket, black T-shirt, black baseball cap. It all provides a stark canvas for the man's necklace, a blinged-out Roman numeral III, that glints when it hits the arena lights just right, and -- "Oh, s---," Pritchard thinks. "That's ..." Allen Iverson looks at Pritchard, Pritchard remembers, and says: "You're the coldest white boy I've ever seen." A CASE STUDY in being cold: Nobody in the league had a better effective field goal percentage on isolation plays than Pritchard last season (58.6%). Not Nikola Jokic (57.1%), nor Shai Gilgeous-Alexander (56.4%), nor Luka Doncic (55.8%). At the midpoint of the 2025-26 season, he was averaging 1.30 points per iso possession (minimum 100 possessions), according to Stat Defender , and had he kept up that pace, it would've been the highest mark for any player in the past decade. Pritchard trailed off in the second half of the season, but according to NBA.com, his 1.11 PPP for the season was still third highest in the league, placing him behind Doncic and SGA. He is the NBA's unlikeliest iso king. And so it only makes sense that in the presence of Iverson, patron saint of undersized iso kings, Pritchard's most urgent thought is this: "That's AI." And his second-most urgent thought: "I gotta turn up. Now I gotta go crazy." The Celtics have been toying with the Sixers' emotions in the fourth quarter, letting them get close late -- down by three points, then one, then two. At which point, with a little more than a minute left, Pritchard decides to break some spirits. "HE'S A KILLER," play-by-play man Eric Collins screams on the broadcast, fittingly, as Pritchard sinks a step-back 26-footer right as the buzzer sounds. Pritchard saves most of his fireworks for Game 4, though, two days later. He nails a one-legged, buzzer-beating 3 at the end of the first quarter; carries Boston in the first half -- he scores 18 points to the starting five's combined 24; and finishes the night with a game and playoff career-high 32. Pritchard does all this from the bench because that's what he is: a bench player. In fact, he's the gold standard for bench players, two seasons removed from being crowned Sixth Man of the Year. Actually, he's a starter in this league, or at least can be, like he was last season for 50 games, after Jrue Holiday departed for Portland and Jayson Tatum obliterated his Achilles. Then again, he's the gimmick guy ( those half-court heaves ) and/or the fundamentals guy ( those viral handles ) and/or the guy who simply rose above his station ( that late first-round draft nod ), who has never looked the part of NBA player. Let alone star -- or sometimes starter -- for one of the league's heavyweights. "He's 6-1 soaking wet," says Celtics assistant coach Sam Cassell, which isn't quite right and is also, somehow, exactly right. If this countercultural iso star is a killer, he's a trained one. For years, Pritchard has held borderline-unhinged offseason workouts that, to those close to him, bring to mind some of the biggest one-name guard icons in the history of the sport. They happen in anonymous gyms, and they're against only those who dare to meet him -- and defend him -- at his level. The Celtics will need every bit of them. And him. Boston leaned on Pritchard's services plenty in the before-times. Before last postseason spiraled into disaster, when the Celtics parlayed a 3-1 series lead over Philly into a nausea-inducing Game 7 loss. Before they sent Jaylen Brown packing in the offseason to -- of all places -- Philadelphia. But now, if the Celtics hope to reclaim their spot atop an Eastern Conference that has grown only more cutthroat, they'll need Pritchard to be even colder. "THERE'S JUST SOMETHING about a humid gym," Pritchard says. It's 6:45 in the morning in the middle of June, and Pritchard has just walked into the humid gym of his choice, at a high school on the southeastern tip of Cape Cod. He'd pulled up to school grounds 10 minutes earlier but had to wait outside while his trainer, Michael Soares, phoned a staffer to open the locked double doors. This gym, like most of the unglamorous gyms Pritchard handpicks for his offseason workouts, doesn't boast amenities such as air-conditioning. A few years ago, a heat wave slammed West Linn, Oregon, where he grew up. Outside, temperatures ticked up to 115 degrees, and it grew only more tropical indoors, hitting 120 in the gym at his high school alma mater, where he was conducting workouts. Pritchard came armed with extra towels because even the ball was sweating that day. The conditions in his Cape Cod accommodations are temperate by comparison. And anyway, Pritchard likes the muck. The muck is why he has been recruiting Division II and III basketball players, international guys and hometown buddies to high school gyms for years now. They're not exactly a ragtag motley crew, but they're not polished professionals either, and Pritchard figures that makes them hungry. He'll pay for their gas to drive down from Boston to the Cape, or their flights to cross the country or an ocean, because they can be counted on to play feisty, relentless one-on-one defense. Today, as ever, it's death by repetition for Pritchard. Bump his defender, create space, shoot. Beat his defender, get to his spot, shoot. React to his defender chasing him. Drive to the basket because his defender is chasing him from too far behind. About 30 minutes in, Bruce Saintilus, recently of Division III Clark University and one of Pritchard's defenders for the summer, is the one chasing Pritchard. He's feeling himself, certain that he has forced Pritchard into a bad angle. But Saintilus runs past the basket, so he doesn't get to see Pritchard attempt an awkward layup. Still, Saintilus knows. He shouts over -- to Soares, or maybe to the basketball gods for forsaking him and his defense -- "Did that really go in?" It did. And so it goes for close to two hours about three times a week throughout the summer. Pritchard will do 150 possessions in his elaborate dance around the basketball court -- the block, the elbow, the other elbow, the 3-point line, the corner, the wing, the high slot, the middle, the opposite slot -- going one-on-one versus a rotating cast of defenders. They'll get breaks, he won't, and if Pritchard shoots under 60% on the day, his defenders eat like kings at Chipotle and then send him the bill. He considers it a small price to pay for the thousands of live looks he gets over the summer, for the chance to square up against one man and try to best him. And then do it again and again, filing it all away in his mental archive. How much basketball data mining is too much? The limit does not exist. "My approach is probably a little different," he concedes. The approach is, in fact, Kyrie Irving -esque if you ask Dave Lewin, the Celtics' assistant GM. Lewin spent the early part of his career in Cleveland, in Irving's orbit, and if Lewin ever walked into the facility at night, there was a good chance Irving was there too, playing one-on-one. "They're obviously different," he says. "But in their approach to playing one-on-one as a form of skill development, those are the two players I've seen do it the most." Pritchard's fixation started early. Back in high school, he would train at ClubSport, a gym near West Linn. He was never a physical marvel -- "unassuming-looking," his old high school coach, Eric Viuhkola, says with a gentle touch. "It wasn't like LeBron James coming through the gym." Still, he caught the eye of another local gymgoer. Steve Blake was nearing the end of his 13-year journeyman NBA career, but he struck up a kinship with the teenager. For the entire summer before Pritchard's sophomore year, Blake would pick him up -- three times a week, sometimes four -- to go one-on-one. Pritchard got beat. And beat and beat, which came as a surprise to precisely no one except Pritchard. "It just destroyed me," he says. "Every day." He made it his life's mission to get the best of Blake by the end of the summer. ("Delusional, right?" says Brian Scalabrine, who became Boston's most beloved benchwarmer in the early 2000s and now serves as the team's TV analyst. "Thinking a 15-year-old kid is going to turn round and beat an NBA player.") Pritchard never did, but he also always chose to come back for more. Because his answer, at least when it came to basketball, was always more. There was another day, also in high school, when Pritchard showed up to Viuhkola's practice with his hands bandaged. His father, Terry, had procured a pair of weighted balls for Pritchard to fine-tune his ballhandling skills. Pritchard dribbled them so much, for so long, they rubbed his skin raw. If he wasn't bleeding -- literally, figuratively -- he wasn't trying. Or at least not trying hard enough, he thought. Comfort became its own brand of discomfort. His high school teammate Brooks DeBisschop noticed Pritchard contorting his body at his desk in class one day. Pritchard explained it was a good chance to work on his hip mobility. Just like his lunch period was a good chance to squeeze in some plyometrics. Pritchard already attended early-bird practices and after-school practices, so he met up with Terry at the high school track during the only free time he had left. Pritchard's justification was that he had read that Russell Westbrook took a huge leap between his sophomore and junior years, and he just needed to hone his athleticism to do the same. There is, Pritchard insists, a straight line from those battles with Blake, and those in-class hip stretches, and those lunchtime plyometric workouts, to his current obsession with one-on-ones. He's the NBA's maddest scientist, and those one-on-ones are a microscope. A chance to put his game under the lens and observe it at an atomic level. In Game 5 of last season's series against the Sixers, early in the second quarter, Pritchard drove hard to the basket then veer stepped Joel Embiid . Eleven inches taller and 75 pounds heavier Joel Embiid. Pritchard put his shoulder into the center, and Embiid flew back a good 5 or 6 feet. "He's knocking Joel Embiid off his spot to get a layup," Scalabrine says. "There's probably a good chance LeBron's not knocking Embiid off his spot to get a layup." Pritchard is strong, but if it seems odd that he's out here defying the basic principles of physics by bodying Embiid, well, that's because he's not actually skirting science. It's just sleight of hand. Or, really, sleight of body. "People always say Payton might be one of the strongest pound-for-pound players," Soares says. "But really, he just knows how to use other players' bodies against them. He truly knows when to utilize his opponents' inertia or speed or direction against them." Because he has tested it thousands of times, maybe double-digit thousands, Pritchard estimates. Against European pros and semipros and guys who are professional practicers. They defend him, give him looks, go again and again and more and more and harder and harder, until that memory has settled into his muscles. Because there is something about a humid gym, and he'll always return to that lab. "HE'S AN ABSOLUTE outlier for what he does," Scalabrine says. Which explains why there's a fever dream-like quality to the Pritchard basketball experience. It's illogical. Here's this 6-1 -- ahem, soaking wet -- guy who lives in the paint, then elbows his way into elite company. Last season, there were 57 players who attempted at least 200 shots in the key (nonrestricted area), and among them, Pritchard ranked third with 56% shooting, after Jokic and Kevin Durant . This guard who doesn't usually get the starting nod almost always gets the nod at the end of possessions. He made 86 field goals with four or fewer seconds left on the shot clock in 2025-26, 12 more than Durant, his closest competitor. And his 51.6% effective field goal percentage on these shots was second only to Jalen Brunson 's 51.7% among players to log at least 100 attempts, according to ESPN Research. This undersized rim threat gets to the basket with power instead of speed, and the only appropriate question is: Huh? "Payton's able to take something that shouldn't be possible, and he can work himself through it to make it not only possible that he can survive, but he can actually thrive," Scalabrine says. "And the only thing you can point to is this: He is a savage, an absolute savage, when it comes to the way he works." In other words, Pritchard is neither magician nor miracle. He's just sort of a zealot, Scalabrine says. In the offseason, when he commits to playing all those hours of one-on-one. In the season, too: The man turns into a hawker after Celtics practice, desperate to sell any takers on playing him -- surprise -- one-on-one. "He's like a lost puppy," Scalabrine says. "'Oh, you guys wanna play ones? You wanna play ones? Anybody want to play ones?'" Last season, John Tonje was headed out of the Auerbach Center, the Celtics' training facility, having just finished a lift and already mentally moving on to lunch. Then an assistant coach called him back inside with some marching orders: Come guard Payton. Tonje, then a rookie, was jazzed to be called to duty. Oh, this is going to be great , he thought. Then Pritchard ran off 17 shots in a row. "The dude did not miss," Tonje says. "It was embarrassing." Nana Foulland, one of the Celtics' player enhancement coaches, started to count off Pritchard's consecutive shots. Tonje would pressure up, then Pritchard would get an angle and go past him. One! Tonje would cut Pritchard off, but Pritchard was already off to his second counter, then pulling up for a contested fadeaway. Two! Boston head coach Joe Mazzulla joined Foulland at the watch party. He folded his arms, which for Mazzulla, counted for excitement, taking in the action from half court as Pritchard went about his dismantling. Three! At some point, Tonje accepted his fate. Unless he blocked Pritchard or stole the ball, he understood Pritchard's shot was going in. Seven! Eleven! Seventeen! "That was my welcome to the league moment," Tonje says. "There was just no missing." BACK AT THE high school in Cape Cod, Pritchard's shirt, which was light gray when he arrived just after dawn, is nearly black with sweat within the hour. He's taking a rare breather, but not a break. Now he's hunched over a laptop with another one of his trainers, Rocky DeAndrade, poring over Brunson film, a forensic analysis underway to ascertain how the 6-foot-2 Brunson became one of the best in the world at drawing fouls. Brunson is fresh off an NBA Finals MVP, so plenty of people want to be more like him. But Pritchard -- diminutive, crafty, iso-dominant and newly Jaylen Brown-less -- might be uniquely situated to make a run at being the next Brunson. Or at least the next Brunson-adjacent. "If he has a season we think he could have, it may be perceived as a breakout," Lewin says. "But I think we'll view it as a continuation of the things he's done well in the past, when given the opportunity. Some of the really promising isolation development and midrange shooting that he had last year, with more of the 3-point shooting success he had earlier in his career." The Celtics will need that perceived breakout or continuation of the things, because someone, or someones, will have to pitch in to help Tatum fill the Brown-shaped hole in Boston. Paul George has entered the fold at 36 and on the offensive downslope, so even if the pitching in is done by committee, odds are good Pritchard will have to be the de facto committee chair. Though this season's (very) early returns have been modest, those in and around the Celtics are bullish on Pritchard's ability to do just that -- "I think he's going to average, like, over 22 points a game," Scalabrine says -- and so, it seems, is the rest of the league. In this year's NBA GM survey, released on the eve of the 2026-27 season, the top candidates for breakout players featured, predictably, a slew of recent top-10 picks on the cusp of their sophomore seasons: Dylan Harper , Cooper Flagg , Collin Murray-Boyles . Also a vote-getter: Pritchard, former top-26 pick, now entering Year 7. These are all reassuring signals for the Celtics. "We've asked him to be more for us every single year," Mazzulla says. "He has the ability to take on whatever the team needs at that particular time, you know?" So, sure, it's never a bad time to tap into your inner Jalen Brunson. It's just that, for Pritchard, for the Celtics, now is the perfect time. And it's not like the Celtics are looking for someone to morph into a world-beating No. 1 option. They already have that in Tatum. Good thing, because even Brunson-adjacent is a heavy lift. One thing about Pritchard is, he loves a doubter. Back in high school, he had a burn book cataloguing his long list of detractors and demerits: too short, too unathletic, too slow, too bad, so sad. His own father earned a spot in the book just by virtue of suggesting Pritchard give some Ivy League programs a look during his high school recruiting days. Even now, there's a scout whom Pritchard still needles because that scout once texted one of Pritchard's college coaches a bleak assessment during the draft process. Don't think he's gonna be an NBA player, he wrote. Maybe a good overseas player, at best a kid named Kevin Pangos. No shade to Kevin Pangos, former Gonzaga standout and two-time All-EuroLeague honoree, Pritchard says, but he was chasing something bigger. So there are people out there who don't think Pritchard has it in him? Good. Great, even, because if there wasn't somebody who declared it a fool's errand for him to chase something bigger, to chase even the likes of Brunson, he'd find them anyway. "There's always doubters," he says. "There's always the next step that people think you can't get to. So you search for that and you find it. "Or sometimes you just make it up." ON THE LAST day of September, with the Celtics two days into training camp, Pritchard and Mazzulla convene in a two-man huddle on the team's practice court. There's a good deal of hand waving, and at one point, Mazzulla sort of elbows Pritchard, perhaps the better to demonstrate the play they seem to be hashing out. It all looks very serious because Mazzulla is famously Very Serious, but then something startling happens. Mazzulla breaks character, then breaks out in a bona fide smile. Mazzulla ... likes Pritchard. What's more, he likes to count on him. "I'll always bet on Payton," Mazzulla says. It wasn't always this wholesome. Back when Mazzulla was still an assistant with the Celtics, he loved to get his hands dirty and play 5-on-5, and one day he wound up playing with Pritchard. The scrimmage got testy, and Mazzulla got frank. You don't make people better, he barked at Pritchard. Pritchard bristled. All he had ever done was work himself ragged. But it was this, his primal need to outwork, to outlast, to outlive, even, that wound up being both feature and bug. One of Pritchard's old graduate assistants at Oregon, Zack Gonzales, watched Pritchard, as an upperclassman, try to break the spirit of a freshman guard day after day. "Payton's goal every day was to make him cry," he says. "He was like, 'I'm gonna kill him.'" So there was Mazzulla trying to tell Pritchard that he was repeating history. He had such tunnel vision to out-everything everyone else that he forgot to bring everyone else along with him. Age and experience -- and a letter later on from Mazzulla to offer an olive branch -- will blunt those sharp edges. Pritchard has a softer touch these days. The timing didn't pan out, but he had hoped to host the newest Celtics in Cape Cod at his workout bootcamp. And he's a little less inclined to kill, though John Tonje would like a word. What can he say? He works how he works. "A menace," said Mike Conley , who joined the Celtics this season, in the early days of training camp. "He's an absolute crazy person when it comes to trying to improve his game." He's a menace because that's what got him here, to all these different versions of Payton Pritchard : The bench star and sometimes starter; the heave god and the league's most unexpected iso god; the new owner of a $44.2 million, two-year extension that will make him a Celtic as far out as 2030. And a cornerstone of what comes next. He's a menace because he has to be. "I can't wake up," he says, "and be Wemby."
